# 1. Introduction

This example applies the similarity structure (SS) to multivariate gut microbiome data. We use PERMANOVA to compare beta diversity between smokers and non-smokers, separately for women and men, and between women and men, separately for smokers and non-smokers.

The data are from curatedMetagenomicData. The default analysis loads estimates included in the package, avoiding the expensive repeated PERMANOVA tests. Set `calculate_ss: true` to run the complete analysis again.

# 2. Read and prepare the data

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5)
```

```{r data}
library(similaritystructure)
library(ggplot2)

distfile <- system.file("extdata", "distancias_full.csv",
                        package = "similaritystructure")
metafile <- system.file("extdata", "meta_full.csv",
                        package = "similaritystructure")

betadist <- read.csv(distfile, check.names = FALSE)
betameta <- read.csv(metafile)

# Some sample IDs contain dots in the distance matrix and hyphens in metadata.
# Change an ID only when its dot version is present in the distance matrix.
dist_ids <- colnames(betadist)
missing <- !betameta$sample_id %in% dist_ids
revised <- gsub("-", ".", betameta$sample_id[missing], fixed = TRUE)
matches <- revised %in% dist_ids
betameta$sample_id[which(missing)[matches]] <- revised[matches]

stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(dist_ids))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(betameta$sample_id))

rownames(betadist) <- dist_ids
rownames(betameta) <- betameta$sample_id

common_ids <- intersect(rownames(betadist), rownames(betameta))
stopifnot(length(common_ids) == 1011L)

betadist <- as.matrix(betadist[common_ids, common_ids, drop = FALSE])
betameta <- betameta[common_ids, , drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(identical(rownames(betadist), rownames(betameta)))

betameta$gender <- factor(betameta$gender, levels = c("Male", "Female"))
betameta$smoker <- factor(betameta$smoker, levels = c("no", "yes"))

cat("Samples:", nrow(betameta), "\n")
cat("Studies:", length(unique(betameta$study_name)), "\n")
table(betameta$gender, betameta$smoker)
```

The four comparisons are:

- **Female:** smokers versus non-smokers among women.
- **Male:** smokers versus non-smokers among men.
- **no:** women versus men among non-smokers.
- **yes:** women versus men among smokers.

These data include 1,011 samples from 10 studies. Some subjects have repeated samples. The following analysis illustrates the application of SS to microbiome distances; it does not adjust for study or repeated measurements.

# 3. Similarity structures

The test is PERMANOVA with 999 permutations. For each comparison, we evaluate 60 subsample sizes and 300 repetitions at alpha = 0.05, with seed = 123456.

The subsampling is **with replacement**, so the evaluated sample size can exceed the number of observed participants in a group.

```{r similarity-structures}
comparisons <- c("Female", "Male", "no", "yes")
N_fin <- c(Female = 70L, Male = 200L, no = 100L, yes = 100L)
num_N <- 60L
num_repet <- 300L
alpha <- 0.05
seed <- 123456L

source(system.file("scripts", "example_cache.R",
                   package = "similaritystructure"))

if (isTRUE(params$calculate_ss)) {

  ss <- list()
  dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)

  for (name in comparisons) {

    if (name %in% c("Female", "Male")) {
      ind1 <- which(betameta$gender == name & betameta$smoker == "yes")
      ind2 <- which(betameta$gender == name & betameta$smoker == "no")
    } else {
      ind1 <- which(betameta$gender == "Female" & betameta$smoker == name)
      ind2 <- which(betameta$gender == "Male" & betameta$smoker == name)
    }

    # The test function takes two sets of rows from the distance matrix.
    ss[[name]] <- similarity_structure(
      betadist[ind1, , drop = FALSE],
      betadist[ind2, , drop = FALSE],
      N_init = 2L, N_fin = N_fin[[name]],
      num_N = num_N, num_repet = num_repet,
      replace = TRUE, test = similaritystructure::adonis_ss,
      test_args = list(subset_choice = name, permutations = 999),
      alpha = alpha, seed = seed, plotting = FALSE
    )

    saveRDS(ss[[name]], file.path("results",
                                paste0("betadivers_", name, ".rds")))
  }

} else {

  # Use the estimates saved with the package.
  ss <- read_example_cache("microbiome")
}
```

# 4. Similarity sizes

The normalized SS can be estimated using either parametric fitting or a binomial GAM. The expected subsample size under each SS is the similarity size (`nS`).

```{r sizes}
ns <- data.frame(Comparison = comparisons,
                 Fitting = NA_real_, Smoothing = NA_real_)

for (i in seq_along(comparisons)) {
  result <- ss[[comparisons[i]]]$simil_struct_Ns
  if (!is.null(result$fitting))
    ns$Fitting[i] <- result$fitting$Ns_fitting
  ns$Smoothing[i] <- result$smooth$Ns_smooth
}

print(ns, row.names = FALSE, digits = 5)
```

## Empirical curves and approximations

Black lines show the scaled empirical non-rejection probability, red lines the parametric fitting and green lines the binomial GAM. Vertical lines indicate the similarity sizes.

```{r curves, fig.width=12, fig.height=3.5}
labels <- c(Female = "Women: smoking", Male = "Men: smoking",
            no = "Non-smokers: sex", yes = "Smokers: sex")

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))

for (name in comparisons) {
  result <- ss[[name]]
  empirical <- result$scaled_bn
  fit <- result$simil_struct_Ns$fitting
  smooth <- result$simil_struct_Ns$smooth

  plot(empirical$N, empirical$scaled, type = "l", lwd = 1.5,
       xlab = "Subsample size", ylab = "Scaled beta(n)",
       main = labels[[name]])
  if (!is.null(fit)) {
    lines(fit$vect_N_fit, fit$fun_fit, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
    abline(v = fit$Ns_fitting, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
  }
  lines(smooth$vect_N_smooth, smooth$fun_smooth,
        col = "darkgreen", lwd = 1.5)
  abline(v = smooth$Ns_smooth, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2)
}

par(op)
```

## Normalized similarity structures

```{r ss-curves, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
colors <- c(Female = "#CC6677", Male = "#4477AA",
            no = "#228833", yes = "#AA3377")

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

max_y <- max(sapply(ss, function(x)
  max(x$simil_struct_Ns$fitting$Sn, x$simil_struct_Ns$smooth$Sn)))

for (method in c("fitting", "smooth")) {
  plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(2, 200), ylim = c(0, max_y),
       xlab = "Subsample size (n)", ylab = "S(n)",
       main = if (method == "fitting") "Parametric fitting" else "Binomial GAM")

  for (name in comparisons) {
    result <- ss[[name]]$simil_struct_Ns[[method]]
    n <- if (method == "fitting") result$vect_N_fit else result$vect_N_smooth
    lines(n, result$Sn, col = colors[name], lwd = 2)
  }
  legend("topright", labels[comparisons], col = colors[comparisons],
         lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.7)
}

par(op)
```

# 5. Comparing the effects with pS

We compare the four effects using `prob_effect()`. The parametric fitting is used for the primary comparisons; the GAM results are also shown. The GAM is normalized over a finite range, so its `pS` can be zero when the other similarity size lies outside that range.

The `pS` is a descriptive comparison probability, not a hypothesis-test p-value.

```{r ps}
ps_fit <- ps_smooth <- matrix(NA_real_, 4, 4,
                              dimnames = list(comparisons, comparisons))

for (i in 1:3) {
  for (j in (i + 1):4) {
    A <- ss[[comparisons[i]]]$simil_struct_Ns
    B <- ss[[comparisons[j]]]$simil_struct_Ns

    ps_fit[i, j] <- prob_effect(fitting_A = A$fitting,
                               fitting_B = B$fitting)
    ps_smooth[i, j] <- prob_effect(smooth_A = A$smooth,
                                  smooth_B = B$smooth)

    ps_fit[j, i] <- ps_fit[i, j]
    ps_smooth[j, i] <- ps_smooth[i, j]
  }
}

cat("pS from parametric fitting:\n")
print(ps_fit, digits = 5)
cat("pS from binomial GAM:\n")
print(ps_smooth, digits = 5)
```

## pS matrices

The diagonal is left blank because we are comparing different effects.

```{r ps-figure, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
ps_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(as.table(ps_fit), Method = "Fitting"),
  data.frame(as.table(ps_smooth), Method = "Binomial GAM")
)
names(ps_plot)[1:3] <- c("A", "B", "pS")
ps_plot$A <- factor(ps_plot$A, levels = comparisons,
                    labels = labels[comparisons])
ps_plot$B <- factor(ps_plot$B, levels = rev(comparisons),
                    labels = labels[rev(comparisons)])

ggplot(ps_plot, aes(x = A, y = B, fill = pS)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(is.na(pS), "",
                             formatC(pS, digits = 3, format = "g"))), size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~Method) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey90") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "pS") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

# 6. Reproducibility

To recompute all four SS estimates, rather than use the results included in the package, set `calculate_ss: true` in the document header or run:

```{r rerun, eval=FALSE}
rmarkdown::render(
  "example_03_betadivers.Rmd",
  params = list(calculate_ss = TRUE)
)
```

The full calculation repeats PERMANOVA with the stated settings and can be computationally expensive.
